analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder for ordinary people to erase credit card and other debts in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill 83–15 in March 2001, but the House never voted on it and it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite bankruptcy law so that people with incomes above a formula-based threshold could no longer wipe out their debts under Chapter 7 and would instead be pushed into multi-year repayment plans. It would require credit counseling before filing and a financial-management course before getting a discharge, lengthen the wait between bankruptcies, and cap the home exemption wealthy debtors could claim. It also includes narrower provisions: stronger collection rights for child support, permanent protection for family farmers, new credit-card disclosure rules, and new protections for banks' derivative and securitization contracts. The Senate passed it 83–15, but the House never voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card issuers, consumer lenders, and other unsecured creditors gain the most: many people who would otherwise have their unsecured debts erased would instead be put on court-supervised repayment plans, and creditors gain new tools to challenge filings and get paid. Family farmers and fishermen also gain a permanent, expanded debt-relief chapter.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card companies and consumer lenders

how_it_helps.text: It replaces the judge-by-judge 'substantial abuse' standard with a formula: debtors whose income exceeds a set threshold are presumed abusive and must document special circumstances to stay in Chapter 7, pushing them into repayment plans under Chapter 13.
It requires every filer to get credit counseling before filing and complete a financial-management course before discharge, and extends the wait between Chapter 7 discharges from six to eight years.
It caps 'homestead' exemptions at $125,000 and lengthens the residency requirement to two years, closing loopholes that let wealthy debtors shield mansions in bankruptcy-friendly states.
It lets any party in interest seek dismissal of a case, expanding creditor power to challenge filings.

analysis.who_pays: Struggling borrowers. People whose income crosses the formula threshold would face higher filing costs, mandatory counseling fees, attorney-fee penalties for their lawyers, and years of required repayment on debts they would otherwise have discharged — even when medical bills, job loss, or divorce drove the bankruptcy.

drawbacks.text: The means test presumes 'abuse' based on a formula and can be rebutted only with detailed documentation of special circumstances, so debtors who genuinely cannot pay but cross the income line face dismissal or forced repayment plans and higher legal costs.

Requiring credit counseling before filing and a financial-management course before discharge adds fees and delay for every filer, and the counseling mandate was widely criticized as an added hurdle that helps creditors more than debtors.

The bill lengthens the wait between Chapter 7 discharges from six to eight years and shortens the look-back for buying luxury goods presumed non-dischargeable, meaning more people stay legally bound to old debts.

The bill itself concedes the lending side of the problem: Congress stated that consumer credit 'may sometimes be offered indiscriminately without lender action to ensure consumer repayment capacity,' yet directed only studies rather than binding restrictions on lenders (Sec. 1230).

Honest critics of the bill acknowledge it grew to include a long list of creditor-favorable provisions — strict dismissal deadlines, automatic eviction-stay exceptions, replacement-value collateral valuation — that go well beyond policing abuse.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine drawbacks: some filers with real repayment capacity do use Chapter 7 to walk away from debts, and a means test with hard documentation requirements is one way to police that; creditor losses are partly passed to borrowers through prices, so tightening rules is not costless to consumers. But the bill's core mechanism — a formulaic means test plus counseling and documentation hurdles — imposed large, recurring costs on people filing in genuine hardship to police a small subset of abusive filings, while the bill endorsed continued indiscriminate lending and did not require lenders to assess ability to repay. The narrow consumer-protection additions (child support priority, predatory-loan defenses, credit-card disclosure warnings) were real but subordinate to the bill's main thrust. On balance, the bill traded a broad burden on honest debtors for modest discipline on a few, which is why consumer groups opposed it so hard.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 83–15 in March 2001, but the House never took it up — the similar House bill, H.R. 333, stalled — and the Congress ended in January 2003 with no law.

narrative.text: The Senate Judiciary Committee reported the bill as an original measure on February 28, 2001, and it was placed on the Senate calendar the next day — an unusually fast start for a bill the Judiciary chair himself sponsored.
On March 14, 2001, the Senate voted 80–19 to end debate and move to final passage; every Republican present voted yes, and 31 of 50 Democrats voted yes.
On March 16, 2001, the Senate passed the bill 83–15, with 36 Democrats and 47 Republicans in favor and 13 Democrats and 2 Republicans opposed.
The bill then went to the House, where it was received and 'held at the desk' on March 20, 2001 — it never received a House vote.
The Senate later pointed to the companion House bill, H.R. 333, but no bankruptcy bill cleared both chambers in the 107th Congress, and the effort died there (a version finally became law in 2005).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people in financial distress came out ahead: the means-test and counseling hurdles never became law in this Congress, so the credit card industry gained nothing. Some consumer advocates also lost their preferred alternative of keeping the easier bankruptcy rules permanently in place as debt loads grew.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-IA), lead sponsor and Judiciary Committee chair's bill manager
for.what_they_did: Introduced and shepherded the bill through the Senate Judiciary Committee and floor, reporting the original measure on March 1, 2001.

for.name: 80 of 100 senators (cloture) / 83 on passage
for.role: Senate majority voting for the bill
for.what_they_did: Voted 80–19 to end debate and 83–15 to pass the bill.

against.name: 15 senators (13 Democrats, 2 Republicans)
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, the only votes on the bill's merits; they were outvoted 83–15 but the bill never became law anyway.

against.name: Consumer and bankruptcy-reform opponents (consumer groups, bankruptcy judges and scholars)
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill as a credit-industry wish list that would punish genuinely broke families while doing nothing about lenders' marketing of credit.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a bipartisan product: on final passage 36 of 50 Democrats and 47 of 50 Republicans voted yes, and only 13 Democrats and 2 Republicans voted no.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: The bill's core function is to route debtors away from Chapter 7 discharge and into repayment, directly increasing what card companies and lenders collect from distressed households. It also leaves intact the credit-marketing practices that produce the debt in the first place.
The bill makes pre-filing counseling a mandatory gateway to bankruptcy, creating a government-certified stream of clients for approved nonprofit agencies while regulating their fees and practices.

Debtors' lawyers face fee-shifting and civil penalties if they file Chapter 7 cases that a court later finds abusive, and non-attorney preparers face new penalties — raising the cost and risk of representing debtors.

industries.industry: Financial firms with derivative and securitization contracts
industries.note: Title IX exempts swaps, netting agreements, and asset-backed securitization assets from the bankruptcy stay and trustee avoidance powers, protecting those contracts' value when a counterparty fails.

The bill permanently reauthorizes Chapter 12, doubles its debt cap to $3 million, and extends coverage to family fishermen — a genuine carve-out for a struggling group inside an otherwise creditor-friendly bill.
